innovations.summary: An RCT of ECPR for selected refractory OHCA reported 20% favorable neurological survival at 30 days and similar outcomes to conventional CPR. This does not establish an instant universal reversal or full recovery for all arrests.

claims.claim: ECPR can restore circulation in selected refractory arrest cases and has been studied against conventional CPR.
claims.scope: In one multicenter RCT of selected 18-70-year-old refractory OHCA patients, 14/70 in ECPR and 10/64 in conventional CPR were alive with favorable neurological status at 30 days; groups were statistically similar.
claims.limitations: A narrow patient subset and no instant single-dose universal treatment.

claims.claim: Safe reliable restoration of circulation and normal neurological function in all cardiac-arrest cases.
claims.scope: Trial found similar outcomes in selected cases, not restoration in all causes or normal neurological recovery in all patients.
claims.limitations: Universal quantifier and full recovery threshold not demonstrated.

claims.claim: Ends preventable death and neurological disability from sudden arrest.
claims.scope: No population-level elimination or impact assessment.
claims.limitations: Impact forecast unsupported.

evidence.supportedClaim: In one multicenter RCT of selected 18-70-year-old refractory OHCA patients, 14/70 in ECPR and 10/64 in conventional CPR were alive with favorable neurological status at 30 days; groups were statistically similar.
evidence.paraphrase: In refractory OHCA eligible for a multicenter trial, ECPR and conventional CPR had similar 30-day favorable neurological outcomes.
evidence.limitations: A narrow patient subset and no instant single-dose universal treatment.

searchLog.outcome: Opened/read primary source; evidence supports only the stated narrower result.

innovations.summary: A seven-day hydrocortisone/fludrocortisone regimen reduced 28-day mortality in a trial subgroup with relative adrenal insufficiency and hastened vasopressor withdrawal. It is not a single-dose cure.

claims.claim: Corticosteroid replacement can improve selected septic-shock outcomes.
claims.scope: A 7-day hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone course reduced deaths and advanced vasopressor withdrawal in nonresponders to a short corticotropin test.
claims.limitations: Subgroup and multi-day treatment; does not rapidly reverse all septic shock.

claims.claim: A single dose reverses host-response dysregulation, restores microvascular function and eliminates infection-driven inflammation within minutes.
claims.scope: The trial tested 7 days of corticosteroids and did not report the claimed minutes-scale mechanism.
claims.limitations: Mechanism, speed and cure claims unsubstantiated.

claims.claim: Dramatically lowers ICU mortality and eliminates prolonged vasopressors.
claims.scope: Trial did not show general or complete elimination of vasopressor use or ICU-wide impact.
claims.limitations: Impact extrapolation not demonstrated.

evidence.supportedClaim: A 7-day hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone course reduced deaths and advanced vasopressor withdrawal in nonresponders to a short corticotropin test.
evidence.paraphrase: In patients with septic shock and relative adrenal insufficiency, 7 days of corticosteroids reduced mortality and sped vasopressor withdrawal.
evidence.limitations: Subgroup and multi-day treatment; does not rapidly reverse all septic shock.

innovations.summary: CRASH-2 found early tranexamic acid reduced deaths in trauma patients with significant bleeding. It does not instantly stop hemorrhage from every source or establish the systemic/topical intervention described.

claims.claim: Early tranexamic acid reduced bleeding-related mortality in a large trauma trial.
claims.scope: CRASH-2 randomized 20,211 adults at risk of significant bleeding; TXA reduced bleeding-related death versus placebo.
claims.limitations: Mortality benefit is not equivalent to immediate hemostasis; protocol was a loading dose plus 8-hour infusion.

claims.claim: A safe systemic or topical agent instantly controls massive bleeding from any source without thrombosis elsewhere.
claims.scope: Trial assessed mortality and transfusion outcomes in trauma, not instant universal bleeding cessation or topical control.
claims.limitations: Universal sources and zero thrombosis risk are not shown.

claims.claim: Transforms trauma and postpartum hemorrhage management while reducing transfusions/mortality.
claims.scope: CRASH-2 studied trauma, not postpartum hemorrhage or all management settings.
claims.limitations: Broad impact forecast not assessed.

evidence.supportedClaim: CRASH-2 randomized 20,211 adults at risk of significant bleeding; TXA reduced bleeding-related death versus placebo.
evidence.paraphrase: In a 20,211-patient trial of significant trauma bleeding, early TXA reduced all-cause and bleeding mortality.
evidence.limitations: Mortality benefit is not equivalent to immediate hemostasis; protocol was a loading dose plus 8-hour infusion.

innovations.summary: Naloxone has controlled trial evidence for reversing opioid-induced respiratory depression. This is poison-specific treatment and does not support a single antidote across unrelated toxins and overdoses.

claims.claim: Naloxone reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression in prehospital settings.
claims.scope: In a blinded randomized ambulance trial, one dose restored adequate breathing within 10 minutes in 79.6% with tested intranasal naloxone and 97.2% with IM naloxone.
claims.limitations: Specific opioid overdose indication; tested doses/routes had different efficacy.

claims.claim: One agent/platform neutralizes opioids, benzodiazepines, acetaminophen, salicylates, organophosphates and other poisons.
claims.scope: Naloxone trial addresses suspected opioid overdose alone.
claims.limitations: No cross-toxin neutralization evidence found in bounded primary-source search.

claims.claim: Eliminates multiple specific antidotes and transforms overdose management.
claims.scope: No broad antidote replacement or population impact was evaluated.
claims.limitations: Impact forecast unsupported.

evidence.supportedClaim: In a blinded randomized ambulance trial, one dose restored adequate breathing within 10 minutes in 79.6% with tested intranasal naloxone and 97.2% with IM naloxone.
evidence.paraphrase: A two-centre randomized trial found naloxone restored breathing in most suspected opioid overdose cases, with the tested intranasal dose less efficient than IM.
evidence.limitations: Specific opioid overdose indication; tested doses/routes had different efficacy.

innovations.summary: In AIRWAYS-2, supraglottic airway first ventilation succeeded in 87.4% of OHCA patients and functional outcomes were similar to intubation. This is a useful option, not an always-successful non-invasive solution.

claims.claim: Supraglottic devices can provide initial ventilation in many nontraumatic OHCA cases.
claims.scope: AIRWAYS-2 reported initial ventilation success of 87.4% with SGA in a cluster RCT enrolling 9,296 patients.
claims.limitations: About one in eight initial SGA attempts were not successful; some cases require other airway management.

claims.claim: A device guarantees oxygenation/ventilation in every difficult airway without surgery.
claims.scope: The trial shows less than 100% initial ventilation success in a selected OHCA population.
claims.limitations: All-difficult-airway guarantee and avoidance of surgical airways not supported.

claims.claim: Eliminates airway deaths and makes management safe for all providers.
claims.scope: Trial did not establish elimination of airway-related deaths or uniform operator safety.
claims.limitations: Impact forecast unsupported.

evidence.supportedClaim: AIRWAYS-2 reported initial ventilation success of 87.4% with SGA in a cluster RCT enrolling 9,296 patients.
evidence.paraphrase: In 9,296 OHCA patients, initial ventilation with supraglottic devices was successful in 87.4%; functional outcomes did not differ from TI.
evidence.limitations: About one in eight initial SGA attempts were not successful; some cases require other airway management.

innovations.summary: A multisite randomized trial found a small PTSD symptom reduction at six months, but not twelve months, after stepped care for injured patients with high distress. It did not prevent PTSD through an immediate universal intervention.

claims.claim: Early collaborative care can reduce PTSD symptoms at six months in screened distressed trauma survivors.
claims.scope: Among 635 injured patients at 25 trauma centers, the intervention produced a small symptom reduction at six months, not twelve months.
claims.limitations: Treated patients already screened for high distress; follow-up effects were time-limited.

claims.claim: An immediately administered intervention prevents PTSD by blocking traumatic-memory consolidation in all critical illness/injury survivors.
claims.scope: The trial tested later collaborative care, not immediate memory consolidation or universal prevention.
claims.limitations: Mechanism and prevention endpoint unsubstantiated.

claims.claim: Reduces long-term psychological disability across trauma, cardiac arrest and critical illness survivors.
claims.scope: The trial studied hospitalized physical-injury survivors and symptom scores, not other cohorts or population impact.
claims.limitations: Impact forecast unsupported.

evidence.supportedClaim: Among 635 injured patients at 25 trauma centers, the intervention produced a small symptom reduction at six months, not twelve months.
evidence.paraphrase: A stepped care intervention for injured patients with high distress reduced PTSD symptom scores at six months, but not at twelve months.
evidence.limitations: Treated patients already screened for high distress; follow-up effects were time-limited.

innovations.summary: A single-dose ED RCT found ibuprofen plus acetaminophen produced pain reduction comparable with opioid combinations at two hours for acute extremity pain. It did not test complete relief within seconds across all acute pain.

claims.claim: A nonopioid combination can reduce acute extremity pain comparably to opioid combinations at two hours.
claims.scope: In 411 analyzed ED patients, pain-score reduction after ibuprofen plus acetaminophen did not differ significantly or clinically from three opioid-combination groups.
claims.limitations: Specific extremity-pain cohort and oral medications; adverse events were not assessed.

claims.claim: Provides complete morphine-level analgesia within seconds for any acute condition without respiratory depression or addiction.
claims.scope: Trial assessed pain score at two hours and did not assess adverse events.
claims.limitations: Speed, completeness, all-diagnosis efficacy and safety outcomes not demonstrated.

claims.claim: Ends ED opioid reliance and prevents chronic pain or opioid use disorder.
claims.scope: Trial did not measure prescribing transition, chronic pain, or opioid use disorder.
claims.limitations: Impact forecast unsupported.

evidence.paraphrase: One ED RCT found single-dose ibuprofen plus acetaminophen and three opioid-combination groups had similar two-hour pain reductions for acute extremity pain.
evidence.limitations: Specific extremity-pain cohort and oral medications; adverse events were not assessed.
